title: Nature of Indian Economy
gist: India is a mixed, developing economy; its main features and reforms.

points.html: Mixed economy: public sector and private sector co-exist; govt encourages both.UPPSC ×4
Blends capitalism + socialism; private property allowed, govt regulates for social aims.
Indian economy = prominent example of mixed economy (not socialist, capitalist or Gandhian).UPPSC ×4
Gandhian economy: decentralisation, equal sharing of resources, self-employment, self-reliance.
Indian model of development protects interest of both State (public sector) and person (private sector).UPPSC
India = labour-surplus economy: huge population, many workers at subsistence wage.
India projected skilled-labour surplus ~245.3 million by 2030.
Underdeveloped economy: low per capita income, low capital formation, high population growth, poverty, illiteracy.UPPSC
Low dependency ratio and workforce mostly in tertiary sector = features of developed economy.
Also underdeveloped signs: unequal income, high dependency ratio, slow national income growth.
India = developing economy (now "middle income developing market economy").UPPSC ×2
Developing features: mainly agriculture, disguised unemployment (extra workers adding no output), poor human capital.UPPSC
Also: low technology, weak infrastructure, poverty, inequality, market imperfections.
Indian economy: agriculture dominates, low per capita income, massive unemployment; industry does not dominate.UPPSC
Lack of natural resources NOT a feature (low labour productivity, low capital formation are).UPPSC
Economic activity: resources (capital, labour) → production → goods/services; e.g. farming, transport, services.
Voluntary social service = not an economic activity.UPPSC
Economic factors of development: natural/energy resources, labour, capital formation, technology, capital-output ratio, organisation.
Non-economic factors: social, religious, political, international, scientific; e.g. social behaviour.
Second Generation Reforms: oil sector, public sector, govt and public institutions; not legal/judicial system.UPPSC

title: National Income and GDP
gist: National income concepts, formulas, estimating agencies, base years, growth data, per capita income and savings.

points.html: National Income (NI) = NNP at factor cost (FC).
NI = GNP(MP) − depreciation − indirect taxes + subsidies.
NNP(MP) = GNP(MP) − depreciation.
NI = NNP(MP) − (indirect taxes − subsidies); indirect taxes − subsidy = Net Indirect Taxes (NIT).
GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad (NFI); so NNP = GDP + NFI − depreciation.
NDP = GDP − depreciation (not plus).
MP = market prices; FC = factor cost; D = depreciation.
National income = money value of final goods and services by normal residents in a year.
GNP: output of a nation's normal residents, inside or outside country.
Open economy: Y = C + I + G + (X − M); X − M = net exports.
3 methods of GDP: product, income, expenditure (no "diminishing cost method").
Nominal GDP: GDP at current market prices, no inflation adjustment; used for GDP deflator.
NDP better than GDP for comparing world economies (shows depreciation cost).
Per Capita Income = National Income (NNP) ÷ total population.
Personal Disposable Income (PDI) = personal income − personal tax payments.
Prices and money income both double → real income unchanged.UPPSC
Problems in counting NI in India: unorganised sector (main), poor data, double counting, non-monetised sector, black money.
Economic growth measured by GDP, GNP, per capita GNP; World Bank aid not counted.
Amartya Sen (Nobel 1998, welfare economics): planning should focus on people, not commodities.UPPSC
Sen's priorities: people-oriented, security for poorest, safeguards on world integration.UPPSC
Hindu rate of growth: term by Raj Krishna (1981); slow ~3.5% national income/GDP growth, 1950s–80s.UPPSC ×3
Economic growth usually comes with inflation.
Labour share in GNP low because wages lag behind prices.UPPSC
Economic growth vs development: growth = output rise; development = growth + better living standard.
Real GNP rise ≠ development if poverty and unemployment increase.
Business cycle: boom (high activity) → recession (gradual fall) → depression (drastic fall) → recovery (steady rise).
Meltdown = steep fall in stock prices; recession = big contraction; slowdown = fall in activity.
Public sector share in GDP declined in decade to 2010; private share rose.
Factors of growth: natural resources, physical capital, population/labour, human capital, technology, law.
Technocrats and bureaucrats = not a major factor of growth.UPPSC
Best measure of growth/development: sustained rise in real per capita income (per capita product).UPPSC ×2
Per capita income represents standard of living.UPPSC
Per capita income growth at current prices > constant prices; constant prices remove price rise.
Real sector: production of goods/services (farming, textile mills); bank lending, bond issue = financial sector.
NEP 1991 strategy = LPG: Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation.UPPSC
Criticism of NEP mostly due to ideological differences.
Liberalisation began with changes in industrial licensing; New Industrial Policy 24 July 1991 (Narasimha Rao govt).
1991 policy: all industries freed from licence except 18.
Dr. Manmohan Singh (then Finance Minister) = pioneer of liberalisation.
Stabilisation: demand side, short-term (inflation, fiscal, BoP); structural adjustment: supply side, long-term, gradual.
Occupational structure unchanged as investment went to capital-intensive industries.
Dadabhai Naoroji: first estimate of national income, 1867-68; per capita income Rs. 20.UPPSC ×2
First scientific estimate: V.K.R.V. Rao, 1931-32.
National Income Committee 1949: chairman P.C. Mahalanobis; members D.R. Gadgil, V.K.R.V. Rao.UPPSC
CSO set up 1951; estimated national income earlier.
NSO formed 2019 by merging CSO and NSSO; now estimates and releases national income.
Capital formation data: RBI and CSO (now NSO); K.N. Raj Committee (1981) fixed roles.UPPSC
Base year: year whose prices are used to calculate real GDP (constant prices).
Base year changed 2004-05 → 2011-12 (CSO, 2015); present base year 2011-12.UPPSC ×2
New series: GVA at basic prices replaced GDP at factor cost; follows UN SNA 2008 (not 1994).
CSO series of Feb 1999 used base 1993-94.UPPSC
Earlier base years: 1999-2000 (around 2009), 2004-05 (around 2010).
Development needs multi-dimensional approach; govt focuses on both micro and macro issues.UPPSC
Macro issues: CAD, fiscal deficit, inflation, employment, BoP; micro: firm, price, consumption.

Balance of Trade (BoT) = exports − imports of goods only (visible items).UPPSC
Net exports = exports − imports; positive = trade surplus, negative = trade deficit.UPPSC
Balance of Payments (BoP): account of a country's exports, imports and other transactions with world, usually one year.UPPSC
BoP = complete record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and rest of world.UPPSC
BoP includes visible trade, invisible trade and borrowings.UPPSC
Current account = BoT + balance of invisibles (services, transfers, net income); capital account = investments, borrowings, assets.

Invisible export = export of services (tourism, banking, insurance, software).UPPSC ×2
Foreigners visiting India (e.g. XIX Commonwealth Games) = export (tourism, invisible).

points.html: Convertibility: rupee freely changed into foreign currency and back at market rate.

Rupee fully convertible on current account from August 1994 (IMF Article VIII accepted).UPPSC ×3
At present: convertible for all current-account transactions only; capital account only partly.UPPSC
Full convertibility = free float + direct exchange anywhere; does not make it an international currency.
Full convertibility advocated to attract more foreign capital.
Capital account convertibility: free exchange of rupee for trading financial assets.
Capital account = foreign loans, FDI, portfolio investment; private remittances = current account.

1991: two steps (1 and 3 July), so twice in 1991-92; ~18% vs US dollar.UPPSC

Devaluation raises prices in devaluing country; it does not cause deflation in importing country.UPPSC
Devaluation does not necessarily improve trade balance (costly essential imports like crude).
Export growth rose after 1991 due to devaluation and export promotion.

Rs 60 → 58 per $: rupee appreciated, dollar depreciated.
NEER rise = rupee appreciation; REER rise = loss of trade competitiveness; higher domestic inflation widens NEER–REER gap.
